entry.title: Welcome to My AI-Native Hackathon Blog
entry.summary: Welcome to the blog documenting my journey in the Panaversity Physical AI & Humanoid Robotics Hackathon!
entry.content:
Welcome to the blog documenting my journey in the Panaversity Physical AI & Humanoid Robotics Hackathon!
This blog is powered by the Docusaurus Blog Plugin, which makes it incredibly simple to publish posts, showcase progress, share updates, and integrate interactive MDX-powered content.

🚀 Getting Started with the Blog​

Setting up a blog in Docusaurus is easy — you just add Markdown or MDX files inside the blog directory.

Each post can include:

  • A slug for clean URLs
  • Authors from authors.yaml
  • Tags for categorization and filtering
  • MDX components for interactivity
  • Images stored next to the post folder

For example, your blog post structure can look like:

  • 2021-08-26-welcome.md
  • 2021-08-26-welcome/index.md
  • With images stored in the same folder (like the one below)

🧠 Why This Blog Exists​

Throughout the hackathon, I’m using this space to document:

  • My progress building an AI-native textbook
  • Integrating a RAG-based AI chatbot
  • Experiments with Claude Code & Spec-Kit Plus
  • Personalization features & Urdu translation buttons
  • Docusaurus tips, MDX tricks, and integrations

This will help me track my development journey and share insights with others following along.

🏷️ Tags & Metadata​

Docusaurus supports tags for smart filtering and organization.
You can define your tags in the tags.yml file, and assign them to posts like this one.

❌ Don’t Want a Blog?​

If you prefer a docs-only textbook:
Just delete the entire /blog directory and set blog: false inside your Docusaurus config.

Thanks for stopping by!
More updates, demos, and AI-powered experiments coming soon. 🚀

entry.title: Exploring MDX + React in My AI-Native Textbook Project
entry.summary: Blog posts in Docusaurus are extremely powerful — especially because they support full MDX, letting you mix Markdown and React components inside a single article.
entry.content:
Blog posts in Docusaurus are extremely powerful — especially because they support full MDX, letting you mix Markdown and React components inside a single article.

This post demonstrates how I’m using MDX, interactive elements, and custom components in my AI-Native textbook for the Panaversity Hackathon.

✨ MDX Superpower

MDX lets you write content like normal Markdown while embedding live React components inside your post.

This makes your blog interactive, dynamic, and perfect for technical demos.

🚀 Why MDX Matters in the Hackathon​

Since the final deliverable is an AI-native technical textbook, having MDX support allows:

  • Interactive examples inside chapters
  • Live UI elements for AI features
  • Buttons for personalization + Urdu translation
  • Custom JSX blocks for explanations
  • React-based visualizations

MDX turns your textbook into an interactive learning platform, not just a static document.

🎮 Interactive Example: React Button​

Below is a simple demo showing how React components work directly inside a blog post.

<button onClick={() => alert('You clicked a React-powered MDX button!')}>
  Click me!
</button>

entry.title: My Complete Journey Building an AI-Native Textbook
entry.summary: This is a detailed breakdown of my experience participating in the Panaversity Hackathon: AI-Native Textbook for Physical AI & Humanoid Robotics.
entry.content:
This is a detailed breakdown of my experience participating in the Panaversity Hackathon: AI-Native Textbook for Physical AI & Humanoid Robotics.
In this long-form blog, I’ll walk through my workflow, tools, challenges, and the major breakthroughs I encountered while building a fully automated AI-powered learning system.

Use a <!-- truncate --> comment to limit how much appears in the blog list.

🚀 Getting Started — Understanding the Vision​

The hackathon is not just a coding challenge — it's a blueprint for how future technical content will be created: AI-generated, agent-enhanced, personalized, and interactive.
My objective was clear:

  • Build a polished Docusaurus textbook
  • Use Spec-Kit Plus & Claude Code to auto-generate content
  • Integrate a RAG chatbot powered by OpenAI Agents
  • Add database + vector search via NeonDB & Qdrant
  • Introduce chapter personalization & Urdu translation
  • Explore reusable intelligence through subagents and agent skills

🧩 Phase 1 — Setting Up the Project Scaffold​

I began by initializing a fresh Docusaurus project.
From file structure to plugin setup, everything needed to be optimized so that the book could grow automatically using Spec-Kit Plus.

Key steps included:

  • Installing dependencies
  • Creating initial docs/pages/folders
  • Connecting GitHub Pages deployment
  • Ensuring the blog and docs systems were clean and organized

Once this was done, I connected Claude Code to the repo.

🤖 Phase 2 — AI-Driven Book Creation (Spec-Kit + Claude Code)​

This was the real game-changer.
Using the Spec-Kit Plus architecture, I generated:

  • Course outlines
  • Progressive chapters
  • Code examples
  • Diagrams
  • Glossaries
  • Index files

Claude Code helped automate formatting, summaries, cleanup, and content alignment.

The result:
A fully structured AI-generated textbook evolving in real time.

🔍 Phase 3 — Building the RAG Chatbot​

To power question-answering inside the book, I set up:

  • FastAPI backend
  • Neon Serverless Postgres for metadata
  • Qdrant Cloud for vector embeddings
  • OpenAI Agents / ChatKit SDK for intelligent reasoning

The chatbot can:

  • Answer queries based on full textbook content
  • Work with selected text snippets
  • Provide contextual suggestions
  • Maintain conversation memory

🎨 Phase 4 — Personalization & Urdu Translation​

I implemented two buttons at the top of every chapter:

✔️ Personalize Content​

Adjusts complexity, examples, tone, and learning depth based on user background.

✔️ Translate to Urdu​

Instantly converts the entire chapter into fluent, academic-level Urdu.

Both features required front-end customization + agent logic.

🧠 Phase 5 — Reusable Intelligence with Subagents​

Using Claude Code, I experimented with:

  • Subagents for code generation
  • Subagents for translation
  • Subagents for summarization
  • Skills that could be reused across chapters

This made content creation faster, smarter, and modular.

📈 Final Thoughts — What I Learned​

This hackathon challenged me to think beyond traditional coding.
I learned to:

  • Combine multiple AI tools
  • Automate textbook creation
  • Build RAG-based intelligent systems
  • Personalize learning experiences
  • Deploy modern AI-powered platforms

This project is just the beginning — the future of education is AI-native.

Stay tuned — many upgrades coming soon! 🚀

entry.summary: The future of learning is shifting toward AI-native education, where textbooks, courses, and platforms are powered by intelligent agents. entry.content:
The future of learning is shifting toward AI-native education, where textbooks, courses, and platforms are powered by intelligent agents. This blog marks the beginning of my journey in the Panaversity Physical AI & Humanoid Robotics Hackathon — a challenge designed to push the boundaries of how we create, publish, and interact with technical knowledge.

Over the next few days, I’ll be building a complete AI-generated textbook using Spec-Kit Plus and Claude Code, deploying it with Docusaurus, and integrating a fully functional RAG-powered chatbot that can answer questions from the book in real time.

Some major goals of this project include:

  • Building a polished AI-native textbook
  • Deploying it to GitHub Pages
  • Adding a RAG chatbot using OpenAI Agents, FastAPI, Qdrant, and NeonDB
  • Enabling personalized and Urdu-translated chapters
  • Exploring multi-agent workflows and reusable intelligence

This blog will document my progress, challenges, learnings, and the evolution of the project as I move forward.
Stay tuned — big things are coming! 🚀
